# ↪️ Pull Request

Solves #1315. When you have two entry points, say index.html and test.html, this code makes sure the server always serves index.html when hit with the folder both files are in, thus mimicking real world server which will also serve index.html by default. 

[This comment](https://github.com/parcel-bundler/parcel/issues/1315#issuecomment-441674707) from me on the issue explains a bit more about the implementation. 

## 💻 Examples

Given the directory structure after a build with two entry points (index.html and test.html):
dist/index.html
dist/test.html

The server should return index.html when localhost:1234/. Current behavior is returning neither index.html nor test.html and hence the request fails.

## 🚨 Test instructions

I wrote tests to test this in. It basically tests if the parcel server serves index.html if two entry points are given.

**However, I wasn't able to test this locally on my Windows machine due to [this issue](https://spectrum.chat/parcel/contributing/only-test-server-js-because-of-test-error~ff160383-9fc5-4a2d-a0d9-0228a578c763), hence the tests should be ran to test if they are correct and don't fail.**

## ✔️ PR Todo

- [x] Added/updated unit tests for this change
- [x] Filled out test instructions (In case there aren't any unit tests)
- [x] Included links to related issues/PRs

<!---
Thanks for filing an issue 😄 ! Before you submit, please read the following:

Search open/closed issues before submitting since someone might have asked the same thing before!
-->

# 🐛 bug report

When bundling and serve multiple entry files, `/ index.html` can not be accessed with `localhost:1234/`

However, you can access it with `localhost: 1234 / index.html`

<!--- Provide a general summary of the issue here -->

## 🎛 Configuration (.babelrc, package.json, cli command)

<!--- If describing a bug, tell us what your babel configuration looks like -->

```pug
//- src/index.pug
h1 hello world!
```

```pug
//- src/sub.pug
h1 sub page!
```

```
$ parcel 'src/**/*.pug'
```

## 🤔 Expected Behavior

<!--- Tell us what should happen -->


When accessing `localhost:1234/`, "hello world!" is displayed

## 😯 Current Behavior

<!--- Tell us what happens instead of the expected behavior -->

Accessing `localhost:1234/` will display empty HTML

```html
<html>
  <head></head>
  <body></body>
</html>
```

However, accessing `localhost: 1234 / index.html` will display the page correctly

<!--- If you are seeing an error, please include the full error message and stack trace -->

## 💁 Possible Solution

<!--- Not obligatory, but suggest a fix/reason for the bug -->

I do not know, but when accessed with `/` we have to make sure to check the existence of `/ index.html`

<!-- ## 🔦 Context -->

<!--- How has this issue affected you? What are you trying to accomplish? -->

<!--- Providing context helps us come up with a solution that is most useful in the real world -->

<!-- ## 💻 Code Sample -->

<!-- Please provide a code repository, gist, code snippet or sample files to reproduce the issue -->

## 🌍 Your Environment

<!--- Include as many relevant details about the environment you experienced the bug in -->

| Software         | Version(s) |
| ---------------- | ---------- |
| Parcel           |v1.8.1|
| Node             |v8.11.1|
| npm/Yarn         |v6.0.0/v1.5.1|
| Operating System |MacBook Pro (High Sierra)|

<!-- Love parcel? Please consider supporting our collective:
👉  https://opencollective.com/parcel/donate -->

review_comments:
It seems like the logic here should be:

1. Is there a file that matches something like `${req.url}/index.html`, then serve that
2. If not, then is there an `index.html` at the root of the dist directory, then serve that
3. Otherwise 404

IDK if that’s kind of special-cased or not, but when you only specify one entry point, `parcel serve` always returns that file for *any* url. In my situations where I have had multiple entry points, I’ve wanted the root index file to be the catch-all and any other specific ones to be accessible directly. My use-case is having an index.html at the root running React Router and another file that lives outside of my react app that can be accessed directly.

Hey @mrcoles, thanks for your review! If I understand you correctly you want the order of resolving to be as you stated in your list (first specified file, then index.html, then 404). 

The thing I don't understand is how that's not the case right now? If I have two entry points, index.html and one.html and I point my browser to /one.html it'll serve one.html, otherwise it'll serve index.html (at least, it should). If you specify only one entry point, this code should always return that entry point, are you saying the code doesn't?

EDIT: I'm on mobile and it's late, I'll take a closer look at your comment tomorrow.

Hey @LuudJanssen it’s possible I’m misinterpreting what `bundler.options.publicURL` and `bundler.mainBundle.childBundles` are, but from looking at just this code it seems like the following edge cases could happen:

1. if there are multiple index.html entry points, it seems like this would randomly pick one of them (or more specifically whichever is the first one in `bundler.mainBundle.childBundles`—is that just how they’re ordered in the cli command?)

2. If there are *no* index.html entry points, but there are multiple entry points, then `indexes[0].name` will raise an error, because `indexes[0]` will be `undefined`. (Also for the sake of consistency, if none are found, it should probably return `null` to match the other case where `null` is returned)

Do you think it would make sense to add some additional tests for when there are multiple index.html files and when there are none?

Oh yeah, I am misinterpreting some of this (I was misunderstanding `pathname === bundler.options.publicURL`), but it looks like there are still some edge cases to handle?

Edit: looking closer at the code, I see Assets have a `relativeName` attribute, so the one at the root has relativeName of 'index.html', while subdirectories would have something like `foo/index.html`. It’d be cool if visiting "/foo" would load the "foo/index.html" file and "/" would load "index.html". IDK if it’s overstepping to have both "/bar" and "/bar/baz" load the root "index.html" too, but that would work well for my use-cases and that’s essentially what the single entry-point code does.

Also, I see the serve code does accept the `--public-url` option and that could break this code too, however it looks like the existing serve code doesn’t support handling it correctly either.
